reason: I attacked the translation first, because that is where this track breaks, and it holds. I fetched the Wikisource page the evidence names and it returns proposition 7 verbatim as “Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.”, credited to Charles Kay Ogden and placed at p. 189. That is the Ogden rendering of “Wovon man nicht sprechen kann, darüber muß man schweigen”, and it is emphatically not Pears and McGuinness 1961, who give “What we cannot speak about we must pass over in silence” - so the wording and the named translator agree, and the usual drift trap is avoided. The locator is right: proposition 7 is the last numbered proposition and nothing follows it, so “the closing line” is accurate and it satisfies the fame test directly (rule 2, the closing line of a work). The attribution is Wittgenstein’s own and the line is not on the misattribution list. shipped.js: no shipped line, no near match, Wittgenstein at 0 of 3, not banned. One correction to the evidence block, which does not touch the card: it gives the publisher as Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner, London, 1922, p. 189, but the p. 189 comes from the Routledge and Kegan Paul printing the Wikisource scan follows. Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner and Co. is correct for the 1922 first English edition, and Routledge and Kegan Paul is the later merged firm, so the page should be attributed to a reprint or dropped.
